lessons.title: When cotton is ready to pick
lessons.html:
When cotton is ready to pick

Cotton is grown in South Africa in warm areas such as the Loskop and Makhathini areas, parts of Limpopo, North West and the Northern Cape along the Orange River. On small and medium farms it is still often picked by hand.

The cotton plant

After flowering, the plant forms green bolls. Inside each boll are seeds covered with fibres (lint). When the boll is ripe, it dries, turns brown and splits open. The white, fluffy cotton then shows. This open cotton with seed is called seed cotton.

When to pick

  • Pick only fully open bolls with dry, fluffy cotton.
  • Do not pick green, closed bolls. The fibre inside is not ripe.
  • Bolls do not all open at the same time, so a field is usually picked more than once.
  • Pick when the cotton is dry. Wait for dew or rain to dry off in the morning. Wet cotton gets mouldy and loses value.
  • Do not leave open cotton in the field too long. Wind, rain and dust make it dirty and lower its grade.

Defoliation

Some farms spray a chemical to make the leaves drop before harvest, so the cotton is cleaner. Workers must not enter a sprayed field until the supervisor says the re-entry time on the label has passed.

Getting ready

  • A clean cotton picking bag made of cotton or jute. Never use plastic bags; plastic pieces contaminate the lint.
  • Hat, long sleeves, gloves if needed, and water to drink.
  • Know the field, rows and where to empty the bags.

Remember: the price for cotton depends on its grade. Clean, white, dry cotton without trash gets the best price.

lessons.title: Picking cleanly and safely
lessons.html:
Picking cleanly and safely

How to pick

  1. Carry the picking bag over your shoulder, with the opening in front of you.
  2. Hold the open boll with one hand.
  3. With the fingers of the other hand, pull out all the seed cotton from each lock of the boll in one movement.
  4. Leave the dry boll shell (bur) and leaves on the plant. Do not pull off bits of leaf or stem.
  5. Put the cotton straight into the bag.
  6. Pick both sides of the row and the low bolls near the ground, so no cotton is wasted.

Keep cotton clean

Contamination lowers the price and can make the whole bale unsellable. Never put these into the bag:

  • leaves, burs, sticks and soil;
  • wet or stained (yellow, grey) cotton - keep it separate if your supervisor asks;
  • plastic, string, sweet wrappers, hair or cloth;
  • green, unopened bolls.

Emptying the bags

  • Empty the bag onto a clean sheet or into the trailer or module, not onto the bare soil.
  • Do not press or stamp on wet cotton.
  • Keep different grades separate if instructed.
  • Cover the cotton if rain is coming.

Weighing and records

Bags are often weighed and recorded for each picker. Make sure your name and weight are written down correctly. Do not add stones or water to increase the weight; it spoils the cotton and is dishonest.

Safety and health

  • Drink water often and rest in the shade.
  • Wear a hat and long sleeves against sun and scratches.
  • Lift full bags with bent knees; do not overfill them.
  • Watch out for snakes, scorpions and wasps.
  • Wash your hands before eating, especially if the field was sprayed earlier.

Key points

  • Pick only fully open, dry bolls.
  • Pick when the cotton is dry; wet cotton goes mouldy.
  • Pull out all the seed cotton and leave burs and leaves on the plant.
  • Use cotton or jute bags, never plastic, and keep out trash and contamination.
  • Empty bags onto a clean surface, cover from rain and record weights honestly.

quiz.question: Why must you not pick wet cotton?

options.text: It gets mouldy and loses value

quiz.question: What type of picking bag should you use?

options.text: A clean cotton or jute bag

quiz.question: What should be left on the plant when you pick?

options.text: The dry boll shell (bur) and leaves
